answer.rationale:
The one memory that could justify the boldest move is memory_c2, so it is the one worth the single verification pull. As inherited, it is the thinnest support for the biggest bet: it praises unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy, but says nothing about on-time delivery performance under load, and it is explicitly about 'last year' at unstated volume. Invoicing accuracy is not delivery reliability. I want the original record to see whether any fulfillment or lead-time data exists, and at what share of volume that switch was made.

Absent that confirmation, switching primary supply is the wrong action this cycle. The binding constraint is not cost, it is that the line runs at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew. A migration inside a 14-day window against a line with no slack converts a price win into a delivery failure, and delivery risk is fenced off by the objective. memory_c3 shows dual-sourcing is the structurally right answer to supply fragility, but it addresses a constrained component, not this renewal, and it does not solve the 18% mandate or the expiry clock; it is the strongest candidate for the next review. memory_c5's deferral worked only because that service was non-critical and had month-to-month fallback, neither of which holds here.

So negotiate_terms. memory_c4 and memory_c6 point the same way from different angles: benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and longer commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. The low-cost quote is real leverage even if I never sign it. memory_c1 says the incumbent path costs no migration work and no interruption, which is exactly what a no-buffer line needs. This keeps supply continuous while attacking cost, and it is reversible.

Uncertainty I am not resolving: the incumbent may not close the full 18% through price and terms alone. If it lands short, the gap goes to the next review as a staged dual-source with the low-cost vendor carrying a small qualified share first, earning volume on demonstrated delivery rather than on a cost claim. I also note the memory set skews toward cost outcomes and is largely silent on quality drift and delivery misses; optimizing repeatedly on the metric the record happens to capture is how reliability erodes without ever appearing in the archive. I am not treating a lower unit price as evidence of lower total cost of ownership.
